newsitem.title: USA: APHIS head says education needed on bunt fungus.
newsitem.headline: APHIS head says education needed on bunt fungus.

text.p: The administrator of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) said on Thursday he hoped an international conference would soon debate the severity of the karnal bunt fungus threat to world wheat crops.

Speaking at the National Association of Wheat Growers' annual meeting, Terry Medley said that by addressing the issue at an international forum in the next six to nine months the United States might be able to raise awareness about the fungus and possibly persuade some countries to relax their regulations against importing wheat from areas affected by it.
"We're trying to see if there are any international scientific symposiums where we could bring this up and make this part of the agenda," Medley told meeting attendees.
Several countries placed a temporary halt on imports of U.S. wheat last March after karnal bunt was detected for the first time in the United States in Arizona durum wheat seed.
USDA subsequently placed quarantines on areas of the U.S. Southwest where the fungus had been detected.
A subsequent nationwide survey by USDA concluded that the fungus spores had not spread into key wheat growing areas of the Plains and Midwest.
But Arizona, California, New Mexico, Texas, Alabama and Tennessee have reported positive tests of wheat with the bunt fungus in the past year, leading to APHIS and state controls.

Karnal bunt is not believed to be hazardous to human or animal health and it does not appear to have caused reductions in harvested quantities of wheat in the United States. It can, however, produce discolored flour with an unpleasant taste.

Several delegates to the convention, particularly those from California and Arizona where the pathogen was detected, privately criticized the USDA for not doing enough to show other countries that karnal bunt was not as originally feared.
But Medley said the U.S. could not expect other countries to ease their regulations about karnal bunt when there was still much that was unknown about its pathogenic traits.
"What we have to do in terms of establishing international agreement that it is a minor, insignificant disease, is not a unilateral decision that USDA or the U.S. can make," he said.

Medley said the International Plant Protection Convention, of which the United States is a signatory, gives the country of destination the authority to determine pests or diseases of quarantine significance. More than 30 countries the U.S. deals with have karnal bunt listed in that category, Medley said.
"We're going to be negotiating to try to change that, but it's not a process that we can do overnight or that we can do unilaterally," Medley told the meeting.

He said the process of asking U.S. trading partners to ease their regulations regarding karnal bunt was compounded by the fact that many U.S. states themselves still maintain strict rules about wheat coming from areas affected with the fungus.
"There's an educational process that has to start domestically," Medley said. "We can't ask people to do something internationally if we are not in agreement and willing to accept it domestically."
Medley said he could understand the precautions still being stressed by some state authorities.

"This occurred in the first 60 days of finding a pathogen that we had never had in the U.S. before -- one that had been prohibited. So it's understandable that those state agricultural commissioners would want to take measures to protect their agriculture until we knew more," Medley said.
"That's the same thing we do now when we impose regulations and we don't allow imports from certain countries until we know more," he said.

Karnal bunt, spread by spores, is difficult to identify. It shows up only at maturity and cannot be detected in plants in the field, The grain must be removed from the head and examined. DNA tests are required for positive identification.
